title: Data modeling in Redis
summary: Mapping domain entities to structures — hash versus serialized object, relationship sets and zsets, live aggregates, hand-built secondary indexes, and hash tags as cluster locality hints.

blocks.body:
Modeling in Redis inverts the relational habit: you design around **access
patterns**, not around entity classes. The exam hands you a scenario — "store
sessions with a 30-minute timeout", "leaderboard with live ranks", "find all
admins" — and expects you to pick the structure whose strengths match the query.

## The modeling litmus test

Answer three questions before choosing a structure:

1. What is the dominant access path — point lookup, range, membership, or
   top-N?
2. Does anything need to expire (sessions, tokens, rate windows)?
3. Who maintains derived data — the app, on every write, or nobody?

The answers usually leave one structure standing. The sections below walk the
standard mappings the exam draws from.

## Entities: hash per object versus serialized string

The first fork in the road: store each object as a hash of fields, or as one
serialized string (JSON, protobuf, whatever your service speaks).

**Hash per object** — `HSET user:42 name "Ada" role "admin" logins 7`:

- Field-level updates without read-modify-write: `HINCRBY user:42 logins 1` is
  atomic and touches one field.
- Partial reads: `HMGET user:42 name role` fetches two fields, not the object.
- Compact `listpack` encoding for small hashes — very cheap memory.
- The TTL story is simple: expiry applies to the whole key.
- Cost: you own field-name governance, and cross-object queries ("all admins")
  need a separate index structure.

**Serialized string** — `SET user:42 "{...json...}"`:

- One `GET` returns the whole object; one `SET` replaces it.
- Plays well with typed codecs in application code.
- Updates become read-modify-write cycles: concurrent `GET` then `SET` loses
  updates unless you add a lock or optimistic concurrency (`WATCH`).
- No atomic field-level counters — every increment is a full-object round trip.
- Bonus: a JSON string can hold structure a flat hash cannot (nested objects,
  arrays) without a stack module.

Exam heuristic: **hash when the app updates fields independently; string when
the app always reads and writes the whole object** — and note the lost-update
risk as the string's hidden cost.

## One-to-many: children plus an index

A parent with many children (user → sessions, author → posts) models as child
keys plus an index of ids:

```redis
HSET post:801 author 42 title "..."   the child object
SADD user:42:posts 801 802            the index (unordered)
RPUSH user:42:timeline 801            ordered but O(N) in middle access
ZADD user:42:feed 1789000000 801      ordered, score = timestamp
```

Rules the exam likes:

- Key each child by its own id (`post:801`), not nested inside the parent, so
  children stay independently addressable, expirable, and lock-free.
- Keep the id list in a set (unordered, unique), list (ordered, allow
  duplicates), or zset (ordered, score = time/rank).
- Never grow a hash without bound: `user:42` should not grow one field per
  friend — move unbounded data into its own structure.

## Many-to-many: sets in both directions

Relationships map to sets keyed on both endpoints:

```redis
SADD followers:42 7 9         who follows 42
SADD following:7 42           whom 7 follows
SISMEMBER followers:42 7      O(1) — does 7 follow 42
SINTER followers:42 followers:9   mutual followers
```

The membership test is the win: "does X follow Y" is O(1) with no index to
consult. Set algebra (`SINTER`, `SUNION`, `SDIFF`) then answers compound
questions without a query engine.

## Relationships with rank: zsets

When a relationship carries an order or weight, a zset replaces the set:
score = timestamp (newest-first feeds), rating, or running total.

```redis
ZADD user:42:likes 1789000000 post:801    liked at time T
ZINCRBY post:tally 1 post:801             live like-counter per post
ZRANGE post:tally 0 9 REV WITHSCORES      top ten posts
```

Bumping scores with `ZINCRBY` builds **live aggregation** in a zset: each event
is one atomic O(log N) increment, and the ranking is maintained for you. A
leaderboard is a zset whose score is the metric; a time-window leaderboard is
one zset per window (`leaderboard:2026-09-03`), with TTLs on the old windows.

## Hand-built secondary indexes

Redis has no query engine, so an index is just another key the app maintains.
The canonical pattern is a set per field value:

```redis
SADD users:role:admin 42        members = ids of users with role admin
SADD users:status:active 42 7
SISMEMBER users:role:admin 42
SINTER users:role:admin users:status:active   multi-field AND
```

- The index is maintained by application code on every relevant write — there
  are no triggers, so a missed write silently corrupts the index.
- Multi-field queries compose with set algebra; that is the whole query
  language.
- Equality on high-cardinality fields (email) uses a set keyed by the exact
  value; **range** queries need a zset with the numeric or time value as the
  score, sliced with `ZRANGEBYSCORE`.
- The trade-off is real: every index doubles the write path and the memory.
  Index what you query, not everything you store.

The relational habit of "index everything" becomes, in Redis, "index exactly
the access paths you serve" — memory versus query flexibility is an explicit
dial, not an afterthought.

## Hash tags: a cluster hint, not a modeling tool

When clustering is on, a key's placement is `CRC16(hash-tag) mod 16384`, where
the hash tag is the text between the first `{` and the first `}`. Only the tag
is hashed — the rest of the key name is ignored for placement.

```text
user:42:followers      slot from CRC16("user:42:followers")
{user:42}:followers    slot from CRC16("user:42")
{user:42}:posts        same slot as {user:42}:followers
```

Modeling-wise this is **only a locality hint**: it exists so multi-key
operations (`MGET`, `SINTER`, transactions, Lua) that must touch several keys
can find them in the same slot. It does not make those keys one entity, does
not balance load — a hot tag piles keys onto one shard — and is invisible to a
non-clustered deployment. Reach for hash tags when multi-key atomicity demands
co-location, and otherwise model keys as if placement did not exist.

## Exam takeaways

- Design for the access pattern; the structure choice *is* the query plan.
- Hash per object for field-level atomic updates; serialized string for
  whole-object transfer, with read-modify-write lost-update risk.
- Children get their own keys; the parent holds an index — set, list, or
  zset depending on ordering needs.
- Sets give O(1) membership and set algebra; zsets add rank and range, and
  `ZINCRBY` turns them into live aggregates.
- Secondary indexes are app-maintained keys: sets for equality and AND
  composition, zsets for ranges; every index costs memory on every write.
- Hash tags influence slot placement only — they buy multi-key locality at
  the price of load balance, nothing more.
